Child abuse early warning system breakdown

By: Viewfinder | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Has the state's early warning system broken down?

Unique Selling Point:
In-depth investigation showing, through a case study, that social workers fail to detect and intervene to remove children from abusive situations, sometimes resulting in the children's deaths/

Summary:
The story will interrogate the failure of Western Cape Department of Social Development social workers to detect and intervene in a child abuse case which turned fatal. Baby CJ Frans was allegedly murdered by his caregiver in Vrygrond near Cape Town in December 2021, reportedly after many months of physical abuse. The Frans family have been on a mission for answers and justice, because they say they had reported the abuse many times in the months before CJ's murder. Their complaints were scorned and belittled by the assigned social worker, they say.

The issue is systemic, and is rooted in social workers' routine reluctance to follow protocols when confronted with reports of child abuse. The attached document discusses our research into this.

The target of this investigation is the social worker assigned to Baby CJ's case, Western Cape leadership of Department Social Development and the National Minister, to answer to the department's failure to maintain a child protection register and to enforce proper "safety assessments" of potentially at-risk children.

Attached also are photos of baby CJ with his mom taken before he moved in with his caregiver (when she could no longer care for him due to addiction). Also, a photo of police removing CJ's body from where it was buried in a shallow grave in December 2021.

Further information:
On 20 December 2021, police and forensic pathology services retrieved 9-month-old CJ
Frans’ plastic wrapped body from a shallow grave in Vrygrond south of Cape Town. CJ’s
family were shocked, but not entirely surprised. They had suspected for months that he was
being abused by his caregiver (who took care of CJ due to his mother’s struggle with
addiction). But, when the family reported this, Dean Bruyns i.e. the social worker assigned to
CJ’s case was incredulous and assured them that he had checked it out, and that CJ was
fine. This, even after doctors identified that CJ had a broken arm during a clinic visit a month
before his death, apparently reporting to the social worker that CJ may be a child at risk (to
be verified). Speaking after the murder, the sister of CJ’s caregivers said that she had
witnessed the baby being abused for months, and had reported this to the family, who took
these reports to the social worker.
On my request, the Frans family has produced a detailed timeline of all their interactions with
the social worker prior to CJ’s murder and with the Department of Social Development,
requesting answers, afterwards. This timeline is backed up by phone records and emails.
The Department says that it has finished an investigation and referred the matter for
disciplinary consideration, but it has not yet responded to family records requests for the
report and CJ’s case file and the report. It stonewalls their queries.
There is every indication that CJ’s murder was preventable. Had the social worker followed
protocol (we have this protocol in hand), acted on the abuse reports and conducted a proper
safety assessment - of his home environment, his physical health, and his caregiver’s
competencies - CJ could have been removed and placed into safe care. Instead, it appears
that the social worker helped the caregiver secure a child support grant – money which the
family now believe was the murder suspect’s primary motivation to become CJ’s caregiver.
We have the grant approval letter.
In the Western Cape, and across South Africa, the failure of child protection social workers
to detect and intervene in child abuse cases is routine, yet has remained unaddressed for
years. To be sure the challenges in the country’s child protection system are manifold. But,
the consequences of this failure in particular (i.e. at the exact point where life-saving
intervention is possible) can be catastrophic.
Crime stats released last week show 306 children were murdered in first quarter of 2022.
The link between unchecked child abuse and the South Africa’s high child murder rates has
long been known. In 2012, a survey of postmortem reports in child homicide cases by UCT’s
Children’s Death Review found that nearly half of the bodies in a sample of more than 1,000
children killed displayed signs of ongoing abuse. But, poor and arguably unlawful (Children’s
Act Section 110) inter-departmental referrals and collaboration between police and social
services means that child abuse cases routinely go unregistered by child protection services,
exposing children to ongoing abuse. This is suggested, for instance, in the massive disparity
between police crime statistics (showing tens of thousands of violent crimes against children:
rape, assault, attempted murder and murder cases) and the comparatively low rates of child
abuse reflected in the statistics the DSD’s Child Protection Register (obtained via PAIA

request). We have done a year on year statistical comparison to show the consistency of
this disparity. In some provinces, the number of child abuse cases registered year-on-year is
zero.
But, what about instances (such as baby CJ’s) where social workers are alerted to abuse? In
the early 2010s, the national Department of Social Development recognized that social
workers had no scientific and uniform process for assessing the safety of children reportedly
being abused. It commissioned experts to develop a Safety and Risk Assessment Tool (we
have and understand the process this tool prescribes). The development process took years
and included immersive reviews of the world’s best child protection systems. Between 2014
and 2015, the tool’s authors ran training workshops to social workers across the country. If
this tool is properly applied during home visits, then children like CJ will not be cleared by
DSD case workers to remain with their abusers. But, cases like baby CJ’s and interviews
with social workers and other experts suggest that the tool’s impact has been limited. Safety
assessments are still being botched because of large caseloads, low morale, poor oversight
/ supervision and a shortage of safe spaces wherein to place at-risk children. This is a
resourcing issue, yes. But, it is also one of unchecked - and potentially criminal - neglect. We
are following up on a lead from a good source i.e. a senior prosecutor of a social worker
currently standing trial for culpable homicide because they failed to act on a case of evident
and eventually fatal child abuse.
This prosecution (to be verified) and baby CJ’s murder throws into question years of DSD
promises and interventions that they say have improved their child protection services’ ability
to detect and intervene in abuse.
A starting point for this apparent turn-around was 2017. In that July year, 18-month-old
Jeremiah Ruiters was raped and murdered by his mother’s boyfriend in Kensington, Cape
Town. It soon emerged that doctors had on more than one occasion treated Jeremiah for
injuries – a broken arm, a badly injured finger – which led them to register their concern with
child protection services. In response to each of these reports, the assigned social worker
concluded (later, by her own admission, based on very little evidence) that Jeremiah was not
at risk of abuse. Less than two months after DSD’s last assessment, Jeremiah was
murdered.
Outrage over DSD’s failure to intervene to protect Jeremiah (the Child Death Review wrote
to then Premier Helen Zille in August 2017) compounded with other civil society pressure on
the Western Cape Government to intervene in the high rates of child murders in the
province. Zille commissioned a study and in November 2018 the Western Cape Government
adopted a “Provincial Plan of Action: Intervening to reduce child murders”. The action plan
identified “Gaps in early detection, referrals, and protection of children at risk” as a major risk
factor underpinned by the failure of social workers to do proper safety and risk assessments,
and proposed a “strategy to reform the child protection system” through a range of
interventions. This was followed by a flurry of interventions aimed at realizing this “reform”:
the Safety Risk Assessment Tool was made mandatory, trainings were conducted, new
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for the removal of at-risk children were adopted.
None of this helped to prevent – in the case of baby CJ – the deadly reoccurrence of child
protection service’s failure to save Jeremiah Ruiters. This Carte Blanche segment will ask

“why?” and suggest that the reason is found in DSD management’s ongoing failure to
supervise and curb sloppiness and procedural non-compliance by its child protection social
workers.
People to interview: Casswell Frans (grandfather) and Melanie Ramos (aunt) about baby
CJ, their experience with the social worker in the months while CJ was being abused and
about their demand for justice and accountability from the WC Dept for Social Development
now (this story will profile the case of baby CJ in depth). Shanaaz Mathews of UCT Child
Death Review project. NPA’s Advocate Bonnie Currie (who oversaw the prosecution of the
Jeremiah Ruiters, and has also seen at least one), Sue du Toit director of George Child
Welfare (who has provided invaluable insight into the inner workings, challenges and failures
of the child protection social workers in the Western Cape). Right-of-reply interview request
and questions to National Minister of Social Development about the failure to properly
maintain child protection register and the apparent failure of implementation Safety and Risk
Assessment Tool). Right-of-reply interview interview request and questions to Robert
MacDonald, head of the Department of Social Development about the baby CJ case,
findings into social worker conduct and the extent to which it throws into question whether
recent assurances that the capacity of child protection services to detect and intervene in
child abuse has been improved.

Press Release:


A tiny grave in the Klip Road Cemetery in Grassy Park outside Cape Town marks the failure of a system that was set up with the express purpose of detecting and preventing child abuse. So, has the country’s early warning system for child abuse broken down? In a powerful and in-depth investigation by journalism watchdog Viewfinder, produced for Carte Blanche, we map how impossible caseloads and poor investigations by social workers can lead to deadly consequences. Could the death of Baby CJ have been avoided? His family believe so, had their reports of abuse by his foster mother been investigated. So, what will it take for South Africa's child protection policies to be implemented?

Script:



Voice over
It is Fathers’ Day, but Caswell Frans is not with his children. Instead, he has come to the Klip Road cemetery in Grassy Park outside Cape Town.

Caswell
I come here more often to do some check up on little C.J. and it is very emotional. Heartbreaking, to be honest with you. My heart has been teared apart. It is very, very sad for me to lose actually someone like that that I really dearly loved. And, you know, it was my only son, actually, my only grandson. I've actually lost a piece of gold. And I never thought it's going to be like that.

Voice over
Baby CJ was born on the 3rd of March 2021. He was small for a newborn, but healthy, despite his mother Candice Frans’ struggle with addiction.

Derek
Was Candice able to look after C.J. for a while?

Melanie
She was only able to look after him for a while because my dad offered his place to come and stay here for some shelter for C.J. She only lived here for two weeks, after which she wanted to leave.

Derek
What do you mean? She wanted to leave.

Melanie
She wanted to leave. They was problems between her and my dad. She didn't want to stay in the house with the baby all the time. After that, Candice actually left with the baby back to the field that she was staying on and still is staying on today.

Voice over
Though Melanie and Caswell were concerned about baby CJ, work and family commitments meant that neither felt equipped to take in a newborn baby.

But, when they heard that Candice had given CJ up for care by another woman in Vrygrond their concerns escalated. Priscilla Morris, CJ’s caregiver, lived in a backyard shack which the family found dirty and crowded during a visit in June last year. They approached the Western Cape Department of Social Development for help.

Derek
What did you hope the department or the social workers could do for you?

Melanie
The things that I had hoped they could do is what they mandate is online, as I checked: to give a child safety that the child’s rights are met, that the child will not be neglected, the child will be cared for and in a loving environment.

Voice over
But, when the assigned social worker Dean Bruyns did a site visit he found Priscilla’s home to be “conducive” for baby CJ, the Department said in a statement.

Melanie
After Dean Bruyns found her willing and able? Definitely there was concern. I spoke to my husband. I spoke to my dad because I was shocked personally.

Caswell
He even promised us actually is going to have a family meeting with us actually, whereby we can take the child back. Because I wanted a child big, I wanted to look after the child. That was my concern because I was very concerned about little CJ.

Voice over
Today Melanie and her family look back on this video with regret. Baby CJ is enjoying a visit with his family. But, on his cheek there is a healing wound: a likely sign that things were way worse at Priscilla’s house than they suspected. Six months later, police made a grissly discovery.

Caswell
Yeah, he was found right here. He was placed in a plastic bag in a shallow grave where his body was broken and forced into the plastic bag, a Shoprite plastic bag.

Derek (link)
This is Priscilla’s family house, the full extent of what baby CJ experienced behind these corrugated sheets and other locations may never be fully known. But, it probably included months of neglect and abuse.

Voice over
Priscilla Morris is now due to stand trial for baby CJ’s murder: just one more case which contributes to South Africa’s astonishingly high child murder rate.

A 2012 study by the South African Medical Research Council suggested that many such victims had suffered histories of abuse. Yet, the large disparity between crimes against children reported to the police and abuse cases registered by child protection services suggest that many such cases go under the radar of social workers.

Voice over
For years Advocate Bonnie Currie-Gamwo led the prosecution of child murder cases in the Western Cape, one of the country’s worst affected provinces.

Bonnie
I think one has to ask ourselves, who takes responsibility for the prevention of child murders? […] I think lots of these deaths could have been prevented, many of them.

Derek
Do you now regret getting the Department of Social Development involved?

Caswell
I really, I really, I regret actually of getting social development involved Derek because I whereby the reason why I say so the social development failed us. If they could have actually listened actually to our, to our complaints and went out and went out automatically actually need to go and do investigation automatically actually this baby will still be alive.

Voice over
But, this was by no means a first. In 2017, 18-month-old Jeremiah Ruiters was raped and murdered by his mother’s boyfriend. This, after a social worker bungled an investigation into reports of abuse, and concluded that Jeremiah was not at risk.

Soon thereafter, the Western Cape government acknowledged that “gaps in the early detection” of child abuse, specifically “poor risk assessments by social workers” was an underlying risk factor for child murders in the province.

Bonnie
I think what stood out for me in Jeremiah Ruiters was that South Africa actually has all these safeguards to assist a child who presents as a child that is in need of care or is potentially in danger. But it also, unfortunately, displayed how children can still fall through the cracks.

Link
The child protection system in South Africa is complex and relies on collaboration between many different agencies. But, it is at that critical moment when abuse is reported to a social worker that a young life can be saved.

Voice over
That moment came for baby CJ. On 14 September 2021, his family received a tip-off that he was being abused by Priscilla Morris.

After CJ’s murder, the woman who made the reports - Priscilla Morris’ sister - told the Weekend Argus that she witnessed CJ being smacked, choked and thrown to the ground. We tracked down Priscilla’s sister in Vrygrond. But she declined an interview because she is a witness in the murder case.

Melanie
My sister and myself, we went through to DSD in Fish Hoek to the offices where the social worker was based. We went to report neglect, to report abuse. He let the receptionist know that we should come back the following day because he's not in office. And I said, we can't come back the following day because we are reporting neglect.

Voice over
The Department has confirmed that Bruyns put no investigation on record into Melanie and Candice’s abuse reports. So, what should he have done? Especially as the department now confirms he had known that CJ had been treated for a broken arm just a few weeks prior.

By law, social workers must investigate abuse reports and take action if children are at risk.

In the early 2010s the national department commissioned the development of a tool to help social workers detect child abuse.

Today, the tool and its life saving potential has been virtually forgotten. Julie Todd is from Child Welfare South Africa.

Derek
But it seems that social workers, especially in government, don't conduct proper safety assessments when abuse is reported.

Julie Todd
I think that is a problem. […] Many of them have very little experience. When I did some training on family reunification pre-COVID with government and child protection workers both in Gauteng and it KZN and discovered that the risk assessment tool was not even known to most of them. None of them had seen it or heard of it.

Voice over
In the Western Cape, the murder of Jeremiah Ruiters and pressure from civil society prompted social development in the province to revive the Safety and Risk Assessment Tool. It, along with several new standard operating procedures, is now mandatory for all child protection social workers.

Link
For years, the Department has known its safety assessments for abused children are poorly done. Policy interventions have been made. But, cases like the murder of baby CJ Frans raises doubts over whether anything has really changed on the ground.

Voice over
Robert MacDonald is the Department’s head who championed many of these interventions.

Derek
So how do you feel when you hear about a case like the murder of Baby?

Robert MacDonald
It's very disheartening to be running an organisation where I'm charged with certain responsibilities by law as the head of department to know that we weren't able to prevent something like this happening. It's something that requires a level of, uh, reflection, and it requires a level of humility in the face of the challenges we're still sitting with.

Voice over
It remains to be seen whether this reflection will lead to real reforms. But, throughout the country, the challenges remain huge: there is a dire shortage of social workers, resulting in massive caseloads which are poorly supervised. And, there are simply too few safe places for children at risk.

Derek
But, Julie to me it seems like a desperate situation.

Julie Todd
It is a desperate situation. I think the system has been collapsing for a while. I think that children are worse off now than what they were 15, 20 years ago because the issues have not been addressed […]I don't think you can blame individual workers. they have no back up and no support. And they burn up and they struggle […] I'm not denying that there will be exceptions, where people haven’t followed through and they must take the consequences of that.

Voice over
Dean Bruyns’ conduct in baby CJ’s case is now subject to a disciplinary inquiry. He responded to our queries in a statement issued via the department.

He did not suspect abuse, because “no suspicions of abuse were recorded” by “medical professionals”. He expressed his “condolences” to the family.

But, did not respond to the allegation that he failed to investigate the family’s reports of abuse in September 2021.

Bonnie
My role as a prosecutor is to determine whether anyone can be held accountable and responsible legally for the death of a child.

Derek
So there is the potential for the prosecution of social workers.

Bonnie
Yes, there is […] In cases of what I would consider gross negligence, yes, I would proceed to prosecute.

VO
For Caswell Frans, justice for baby CJ will only be complete through measures to protect other children at risk of abuse.

Caswell
It's not about C.J. now any longer because he is no longer. But my concern is about the other children, and that is also actually now actually being abused. That is also being actually neglected whereby because the people tried to get and inform actually social workers, because we trust in them, because it is a daily work, it is their passion.

This Carte Blanche segment will ask “why?” and suggest that the reason is found in DSD management’s ongoing failure to supervise and curb sloppiness and procedural non-compliance by its child protection social workers. So, has the country’s early warning system for child abuse broken down? In a powerful and in-depth investigation by journalism watchdog Viewfinder, produced for Carte Blanche, we map how impossible caseloads and poor investigations by social workers can lead to deadly consequences. Could the death of Baby CJ have been avoided? His family believe so, had their reports of abuse by his foster mother been investigated. So, what will it take for South Africa's child protection policies to be implemented? Script: Voice over It is Fathers’ Day, but Caswell Frans is not with his children. Instead, he has come to the Klip Road cemetery in Grassy Park outside Cape Town. Caswell I come here more often to do some check up on little C.J. and it is very emotional. Heartbreaking, to be honest with you. My heart has been teared apart. It is very, very sad for me to lose actually someone like that that I really dearly loved. And, you know, it was my only son, actually, my only grandson. I've actually lost a piece of gold. And I never thought it's going to be like that. Voice over Baby CJ was born on the 3rd of March 2021. He was small for a newborn, but healthy, despite his mother Candice Frans’ struggle with addiction. Derek Was Candice able to look after C.J. for a while? Melanie She was only able to look after him for a while because my dad offered his place to come and stay here for some shelter for C.J. She only lived here for two weeks, after which she wanted to leave. Derek What do you mean? She wanted to leave. Melanie She wanted to leave. They was problems between her and my dad. She didn't want to stay in the house with the baby all the time. After that, Candice actually left with the baby back to the field that she was staying on and still is staying on today. Voice over Though Melanie and Caswell were concerned about baby CJ, work and family commitments meant that neither felt equipped to take in a newborn baby. But, when they heard that Candice had given CJ up for care by another woman in Vrygrond their concerns escalated. Priscilla Morris, CJ’s caregiver, lived in a backyard shack which the family found dirty and crowded during a visit in June last year. They approached the Western Cape Department of Social Development for help. Derek What did you hope the department or the social workers could do for you? Melanie The things that I had hoped they could do is what they mandate is online, as I checked: to give a child safety that the child’s rights are met, that the child will not be neglected, the child will be cared for and in a loving environment. Voice over But, when the assigned social worker Dean Bruyns did a site visit he found Priscilla’s home to be “conducive” for baby CJ, the Department said in a statement. Melanie After Dean Bruyns found her willing and able? Definitely there was concern. I spoke to my husband. I spoke to my dad because I was shocked personally. Caswell He even promised us actually is going to have a family meeting with us actually, whereby we can take the child back. Because I wanted a child big, I wanted to look after the child. That was my concern because I was very concerned about little CJ. Voice over Today Melanie and her family look back on this video with regret. Baby CJ is enjoying a visit with his family. But, on his cheek there is a healing wound: a likely sign that things were way worse at Priscilla’s house than they suspected. Six months later, police made a grissly discovery. Caswell Yeah, he was found right here. He was placed in a plastic bag in a shallow grave where his body was broken and forced into the plastic bag, a Shoprite plastic bag. Derek (link) This is Priscilla’s family house, the full extent of what baby CJ experienced behind these corrugated sheets and other locations may never be fully known. But, it probably included months of neglect and abuse. Voice over Priscilla Morris is now due to stand trial for baby CJ’s murder: just one more case which contributes to South Africa’s astonishingly high child murder rate. A 2012 study by the South African Medical Research Council suggested that many such victims had suffered histories of abuse. Yet, the large disparity between crimes against children reported to the police and abuse cases registered by child protection services suggest that many such cases go under the radar of social workers. Voice over For years Advocate Bonnie Currie-Gamwo led the prosecution of child murder cases in the Western Cape, one of the country’s worst affected provinces. Bonnie I think one has to ask ourselves, who takes responsibility for the prevention of child murders? […] I think lots of these deaths could have been prevented, many of them. Derek Do you now regret getting the Department of Social Development involved? Caswell I really, I really, I regret actually of getting social development involved Derek because I whereby the reason why I say so the social development failed us. If they could have actually listened actually to our, to our complaints and went out and went out automatically actually need to go and do investigation automatically actually this baby will still be alive. Voice over But, this was by no means a first. In 2017, 18-month-old Jeremiah Ruiters was raped and murdered by his mother’s boyfriend. This, after a social worker bungled an investigation into reports of abuse, and concluded that Jeremiah was not at risk. Soon thereafter, the Western Cape government acknowledged that “gaps in the early detection” of child abuse, specifically “poor risk assessments by social workers” was an underlying risk factor for child murders in the province. Bonnie I think what stood out for me in Jeremiah Ruiters was that South Africa actually has all these safeguards to assist a child who presents as a child that is in need of care or is potentially in danger. But it also, unfortunately, displayed how children can still fall through the cracks. Link The child protection system in South Africa is complex and relies on collaboration between many different agencies. But, it is at that critical moment when abuse is reported to a social worker that a young life can be saved. Voice over That moment came for baby CJ. On 14 September 2021, his family received a tip-off that he was being abused by Priscilla Morris. After CJ’s murder, the woman who made the reports - Priscilla Morris’ sister - told the Weekend Argus that she witnessed CJ being smacked, choked and thrown to the ground. We tracked down Priscilla’s sister in Vrygrond. But she declined an interview because she is a witness in the murder case. Melanie My sister and myself, we went through to DSD in Fish Hoek to the offices where the social worker was based. We went to report neglect, to report abuse. He let the receptionist know that we should come back the following day because he's not in office. And I said, we can't come back the following day because we are reporting neglect. Voice over The Department has confirmed that Bruyns put no investigation on record into Melanie and Candice’s abuse reports. So, what should he have done? Especially as the department now confirms he had known that CJ had been treated for a broken arm just a few weeks prior. By law, social workers must investigate abuse reports and take action if children are at risk. In the early 2010s the national department commissioned the development of a tool to help social workers detect child abuse. Today, the tool and its life saving potential has been virtually forgotten. Julie Todd is from Child Welfare South Africa. Derek But it seems that social workers, especially in government, don't conduct proper safety assessments when abuse is reported. Julie Todd I think that is a problem. […] Many of them have very little experience. When I did some training on family reunification pre-COVID with government and child protection workers both in Gauteng and it KZN and discovered that the risk assessment tool was not even known to most of them. None of them had seen it or heard of it. Voice over In the Western Cape, the murder of Jeremiah Ruiters and pressure from civil society prompted social development in the province to revive the Safety and Risk Assessment Tool. It, along with several new standard operating procedures, is now mandatory for all child protection social workers. Link For years, the Department has known its safety assessments for abused children are poorly done. Policy interventions have been made. But, cases like the murder of baby CJ Frans raises doubts over whether anything has really changed on the ground. Voice over Robert MacDonald is the Department’s head who championed many of these interventions. Derek So how do you feel when you hear about a case like the murder of Baby? Robert MacDonald It's very disheartening to be running an organisation where I'm charged with certain responsibilities by law as the head of department to know that we weren't able to prevent something like this happening. It's something that requires a level of, uh, reflection, and it requires a level of humility in the face of the challenges we're still sitting with. Voice over It remains to be seen whether this reflection will lead to real reforms. But, throughout the country, the challenges remain huge: there is a dire shortage of social workers, resulting in massive caseloads which are poorly supervised. And, there are simply too few safe places for children at risk. Derek But, Julie to me it seems like a desperate situation. Julie Todd It is a desperate situation. I think the system has been collapsing for a while. I think that children are worse off now than what they were 15, 20 years ago because the issues have not been addressed […]I don't think you can blame individual workers. they have no back up and no support. And they burn up and they struggle […] I'm not denying that there will be exceptions, where people haven’t followed through and they must take the consequences of that. Voice over Dean Bruyns’ conduct in baby CJ’s case is now subject to a disciplinary inquiry. He responded to our queries in a statement issued via the department. He did not suspect abuse, because “no suspicions of abuse were recorded” by “medical professionals”. He expressed his “condolences” to the family. But, did not respond to the allegation that he failed to investigate the family’s reports of abuse in September 2021. Bonnie My role as a prosecutor is to determine whether anyone can be held accountable and responsible legally for the death of a child. Derek So there is the potential for the prosecution of social workers. Bonnie Yes, there is […] In cases of what I would consider gross negligence, yes, I would proceed to prosecute. VO For Caswell Frans, justice for baby CJ will only be complete through measures to protect other children at risk of abuse. Caswell It's not about C.J. now any longer because he is no longer. But my concern is about the other children, and that is also actually now actually being abused. That is also being actually neglected whereby because the people tried to get and inform actually social workers, because we trust in them, because it is a daily work, it is their passion. metadata.Unique Selling Point: In-depth investigation showing, through a case study, that social workers fail to detect and intervene to remove children from abusive situations, sometimes resulting in the children's deaths/
metadata.Summary: The story will interrogate the failure of Western Cape Department of Social Development social workers to detect and intervene in a child abuse case which turned fatal. Baby CJ Frans was allegedly murdered by his caregiver in Vrygrond near Cape Town in December 2021, reportedly after many months of physical abuse. The Frans family have been on a mission for answers and justice, because they say they had reported the abuse many times in the months before CJ's murder. Their complaints were scorned and belittled by the assigned social worker, they say. The issue is systemic, and is rooted in social workers' routine reluctance to follow protocols when confronted with reports of child abuse. The attached document discusses our research into this. The target of this investigation is the social worker assigned to Baby CJ's case, Western Cape leadership of Department Social Development and the National Minister, to answer to the department's failure to maintain a child protection register and to enforce proper "safety assessments" of potentially at-risk children. Attached also are photos of baby CJ with his mom taken before he moved in with his caregiver (when she could no longer care for him due to addiction). Also, a photo of police removing CJ's body from where it was buried in a shallow grave in December 2021.
metadata.Further information: On 20 December 2021, police and forensic pathology services retrieved 9-month-old CJ Frans’ plastic wrapped body from a shallow grave in Vrygrond south of Cape Town. CJ’s family were shocked, but not entirely surprised. They had suspected for months that he was being abused by his caregiver (who took care of CJ due to his mother’s struggle with addiction). But, when the family reported this, Dean Bruyns i.e. the social worker assigned to CJ’s case was incredulous and assured them that he had checked it out, and that CJ was fine. This, even after doctors identified that CJ had a broken arm during a clinic visit a month before his death, apparently reporting to the social worker that CJ may be a child at risk (to be verified). Speaking after the murder, the sister of CJ’s caregivers said that she had witnessed the baby being abused for months, and had reported this to the family, who took these reports to the social worker. On my request, the Frans family has produced a detailed timeline of all their interactions with the social worker prior to CJ’s murder and with the Department of Social Development, requesting answers, afterwards. This timeline is backed up by phone records and emails. The Department says that it has finished an investigation and referred the matter for disciplinary consideration, but it has not yet responded to family records requests for the report and CJ’s case file and the report. It stonewalls their queries. There is every indication that CJ’s murder was preventable. Had the social worker followed protocol (we have this protocol in hand), acted on the abuse reports and conducted a proper safety assessment - of his home environment, his physical health, and his caregiver’s competencies - CJ could have been removed and placed into safe care. Instead, it appears that the social worker helped the caregiver secure a child support grant – money which the family now believe was the murder suspect’s primary motivation to become CJ’s caregiver. We have the grant approval letter. In the Western Cape, and across South Africa, the failure of child protection social workers to detect and intervene in child abuse cases is routine, yet has remained unaddressed for years. To be sure the challenges in the country’s child protection system are manifold. But, the consequences of this failure in particular (i.e. at the exact point where life-saving intervention is possible) can be catastrophic. Crime stats released last week show 306 children were murdered in first quarter of 2022. The link between unchecked child abuse and the South Africa’s high child murder rates has long been known. In 2012, a survey of postmortem reports in child homicide cases by UCT’s Children’s Death Review found that nearly half of the bodies in a sample of more than 1,000 children killed displayed signs of ongoing abuse. But, poor and arguably unlawful (Children’s Act Section 110) inter-departmental referrals and collaboration between police and social services means that child abuse cases routinely go unregistered by child protection services, exposing children to ongoing abuse. This is suggested, for instance, in the massive disparity between police crime statistics (showing tens of thousands of violent crimes against children: rape, assault, attempted murder and murder cases) and the comparatively low rates of child abuse reflected in the statistics the DSD’s Child Protection Register (obtained via PAIA request). We have done a year on year statistical comparison to show the consistency of this disparity. In some provinces, the number of child abuse cases registered year-on-year is zero. But, what about instances (such as baby CJ’s) where social workers are alerted to abuse? In the early 2010s, the national Department of Social Development recognized that social workers had no scientific and uniform process for assessing the safety of children reportedly being abused. It commissioned experts to develop a Safety and Risk Assessment Tool (we have and understand the process this tool prescribes). The development process took years and included immersive reviews of the world’s best child protection systems. Between 2014 and 2015, the tool’s authors ran training workshops to social workers across the country. If this tool is properly applied during home visits, then children like CJ will not be cleared by DSD case workers to remain with their abusers. But, cases like baby CJ’s and interviews with social workers and other experts suggest that the tool’s impact has been limited. Safety assessments are still being botched because of large caseloads, low morale, poor oversight / supervision and a shortage of safe spaces wherein to place at-risk children. This is a resourcing issue, yes. But, it is also one of unchecked - and potentially criminal - neglect. We are following up on a lead from a good source i.e. a senior prosecutor of a social worker currently standing trial for culpable homicide because they failed to act on a case of evident and eventually fatal child abuse. This prosecution (to be verified) and baby CJ’s murder throws into question years of DSD promises and interventions that they say have improved their child protection services’ ability to detect and intervene in abuse. A starting point for this apparent turn-around was 2017. In that July year, 18-month-old Jeremiah Ruiters was raped and murdered by his mother’s boyfriend in Kensington, Cape Town. It soon emerged that doctors had on more than one occasion treated Jeremiah for injuries – a broken arm, a badly injured finger – which led them to register their concern with child protection services. In response to each of these reports, the assigned social worker concluded (later, by her own admission, based on very little evidence) that Jeremiah was not at risk of abuse. Less than two months after DSD’s last assessment, Jeremiah was murdered. Outrage over DSD’s failure to intervene to protect Jeremiah (the Child Death Review wrote to then Premier Helen Zille in August 2017) compounded with other civil society pressure on the Western Cape Government to intervene in the high rates of child murders in the province. Zille commissioned a study and in November 2018 the Western Cape Government adopted a “Provincial Plan of Action: Intervening to reduce child murders”. The action plan identified “Gaps in early detection, referrals, and protection of children at risk” as a major risk factor underpinned by the failure of social workers to do proper safety and risk assessments, and proposed a “strategy to reform the child protection system” through a range of interventions. This was followed by a flurry of interventions aimed at realizing this “reform”: the Safety Risk Assessment Tool was made mandatory, trainings were conducted, new Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for the removal of at-risk children were adopted. None of this helped to prevent – in the case of baby CJ – the deadly reoccurrence of child protection service’s failure to save Jeremiah Ruiters. This Carte Blanche segment will ask “why?” and suggest that the reason is found in DSD management’s ongoing failure to supervise and curb sloppiness and procedural non-compliance by its child protection social workers. People to interview: Casswell Frans (grandfather) and Melanie Ramos (aunt) about baby CJ, their experience with the social worker in the months while CJ was being abused and about their demand for justice and accountability from the WC Dept for Social Development now (this story will profile the case of baby CJ in depth). Shanaaz Mathews of UCT Child Death Review project. NPA’s Advocate Bonnie Currie (who oversaw the prosecution of the Jeremiah Ruiters, and has also seen at least one), Sue du Toit director of George Child Welfare (who has provided invaluable insight into the inner workings, challenges and failures of the child protection social workers in the Western Cape). Right-of-reply interview request and questions to National Minister of Social Development about the failure to properly maintain child protection register and the apparent failure of implementation Safety and Risk Assessment Tool).
